answer:
1000 SCFM of natural gas is about 1607 Nm³/h. This assumes the usual US standard of 60°F and 14.696 psia for SCFM, and 0°C and 101.325 kPa for Nm³.

How it works out:
- 1000 ft³/min × 0.0283168 m³/ft³ × 60 min/h = 1699.0 m³/h at 60°F and 1 atm.
- Correcting from 60°F to 0°C multiplies by 273.15 / 288.71 = 0.9461, which gives **1607.5 Nm³/h**.
- Both standards are at 1 atm (14.696 psia is 101.325 kPa), so no pressure correction is needed.

The answer depends on which standard the SCFM figure uses:
| SCFM reference | Nm³/h |
|---|---|
| 60°F, 14.696 psia (most common) | 1607.5 |
| 60°F, 14.73 psia (US gas billing standard) | 1611.2 |
| 68°F, 14.696 psia | 1583.1 |
| 70°F, 14.696 psia | 1577.1 |

This is a volume-to-volume conversion using the ideal-gas law, so it doesn't depend on the gas composition. Treating natural gas as non-ideal changes the result by less than about 0.1% at standard conditions; I estimated that and did not calculate it. I checked the numbers in the table with a short Python script. No files were created.
